We argue that continuous diffusion can effectively model discrete sequences through the joint design of noise parameterization and token representation geometry. We introduce \emph{Discrete Stochastic Localization} (DSL), a continuous-state framework that combines a stochastic localization channel with unit-sphere token embeddings, resulting in a Bayes-optimal denoiser that depends only on the noisy state, without additional timestep conditioning. A single trained denoising network then supports multiple sampling methods, from continuous denoising to masked diffusion, random-order autoregressive generation and hybrid continuous-then-discrete generation. Parallel generation in this continuous-state framework, therefore, need not imply synchronized denoising: some tokens can establish context earlier while others remain open to refinement. Fine-tuning a pretrained MDLM checkpoint with DSL substantially improves generation quality, as measured by MAUVE, on OpenWebText across all step budgets from $T{=}128$ to $T{=}1024$. The same checkpoint supports random-order autoregressive sampling, and a hybrid continuous-then-discrete sampler using as few as $T=48$ total steps, without distillation or further training.

Machine Learning.title: How do features act in an individual prediction? Separating standalone and interaction effects with a case-based taxonomy
Machine Learning.summary: Local explanation methods such as SHAP and LIME summarize each feature with a single attribution score, and interaction indices quantify how strongly features interact. Neither tells a user how a feature acts in a given prediction: whether its effect is the same alone and in context, or whether the other features amplify it, make it unnecessary, switch it off or reverse it. We extend case-based feature importance (CBFI), originally a global method, to individual predictions. Evaluating the model in four hybrid states per background sample decomposes the in-context importance of a feature into a standalone and an interaction effect, and a case taxonomy labels each feature of an instance as inactive, standalone, amplified, redundant, gated or reversed. We compare the method with k-SII, TreeSHAP interaction values and the H-statistic on synthetic functions, and study eight real tabular datasets with six model families. On the true functions, the decomposition recovered interactions exactly (correlation 0.99 with the analytic local interaction). On fitted models, pair recovery was slightly below that of dedicated indices (local precision@k 0.86-0.91 versus 0.91-0.95). Interaction values alone could not distinguish substitution from gating, whereas the taxonomy identified both without knowing the partner (accuracy 0.74-0.76); applied to Shapley interaction values, it performed comparably. On real data, 45-57% of feature pairs with nearly identical SHAP values received different labels, and in a medical-insurance model the method showed that the interaction component of smoking changes sign at a body-mass index of 30. Localized CBFI does not detect interactions more accurately than existing indices; what it adds is a decomposition into standalone and interaction effects and a label stating how each feature acts.

Machine Learning.title: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration
Machine Learning.summary: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.
Machine Learning.comment: 18 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Project page: https://heaveho-humanoid.github.io/

Machine Learning.title: The multiplicative Lipschitz bound as an inductive bias
Machine Learning.summary: We study the problem of training a neural network to minimize a loss function given a Lipschitz constraint. While the most obvious way to estimate the Lipschitz constant of a neural network is to multiply the Lipschitz constants of its layers, this bound, which we term the _trivial bound_, is often considered impractically loose. We show that, on the contrary, it can be more effective than state-of-the-art methods (Sandwich, Almost-Orthogonal Layers, Convex Potential Layers, and SDP-based Lipschitz Layers) for Lipschitz-constrained learning. Our method combines the trivial bound with a novel activation function (the quadrature nonlinearity) to achieve lower cross-entropy over most of the tested classification bounds. For autoencoders constrained to be nonexpansive in a learned norm, it achieves the lowest pixel reconstruction error at every tested bottleneck width, improving on PCA by 12--24%. Our architecture, consisting of concatenated cosine and sine activations, is supported by a semi-rigorous theoretical analysis of Lipschitz bound looseness that may prove valuable in its own right.

Machine Learning.title: How Complete Must an Environment Be to Train a Capable GUI Agent?
Machine Learning.summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are widely trained in executable GUI environments. To lower cost, build environments in batches, and reduce manual effort, each work trades away part of the environment through its construction choices. We describe these choices along three dimensions: reward coverage, the goal-reaching trajectories the verifier rewards; data coverage, the application data the agent is exposed to beyond what the task reads or writes; and feature coverage, the application features beyond what the task uses. Existing works set each dimension on engineering grounds, but they do not measure its effect on training. How complete must an environment be to train a capable agent, and along which dimensions? In MobileGym, we adjust each dimension separately, train Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, and evaluate every policy in the original full environment. A verifier that rewards only one reference path lowers success by 10.53 points, and removing unneeded records also lowers success. Pruning unneeded features instead raises success from 51.61% to 56.13%, entirely on tasks whose environments it left unchanged. The gain reverses when each episode is weighted equally and vanishes when only episodes on the pruned tasks are balanced. Without pruning, length weighting there reinforces long detour successes that erode skills on other tasks. Following these findings, we build MobileGym-Lite, which keeps reward and data coverage complete and prunes unneeded features. It outperforms Full in the full environment (55.48% versus 51.61% success) with lower construction cost.

Machine Learning.title: PGU-Decoder: Prior-Guided Unified Decoding for Industrial Road-Network Map Updating
Machine Learning.summary: Timely road-network map updates are essential to navigation and autonomous driving. Three key tasks are intra-intersection road network generation, merging/diverging detection, and drivable-area detection, covering topology, geometry, and attributes, respectively. Separate pipelines duplicate rule maintenance, quality assurance, and manual verification, increasing operational costs. We propose PGU-Decoder, a production-grade unified decoding framework for semantic prediction across these tasks. A Prior Query Module (PQM) constructs point-level prior queries from sampled locations on road-network geometries. Fixed reference points preserve positional priors throughout decoding, allowing the model to focus on surrounding context. Point-level representations are aggregated into instance-level representations, and a Relational Graph Attention Network (RGAT) captures inter-instance dependencies. Task-specific heads then generate predictions. We validate PGU-Decoder in large-scale automated road-network map updating across more than 360 cities in China, where it consistently outperforms seven baselines. Following deployment at AutoNavi Map, it achieves quality scores above 98% on all three tasks, reduces manual verification costs by 95%, and increases update frequency from weekly to hourly. These results demonstrate a practical and cost-effective industrial solution for road-network map updating.
Machine Learning.comment: 11 pages. Accepted at KDD 2027, Applied Data Science (ADS) Track. This is the original submission version, prior to reviewer revisions

Machine Learning.title: LoongSage: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train-inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.

Machine Learning.title: Graph-of-Thoughts for LLM Causal Discovery with a Fairness-Pathway Case Study
Machine Learning.summary: Methods that use large language models (LLMs) for causal discovery reason locally, deciding one variable pair or one node at a time, so they never compare alternative whole graphs. We introduce GoT-CD, a Graph-of-Thoughts method that asks an LLM for several complete candidate graphs from variable metadata alone, ranks them with a deterministic validity score, merges them under a hard union constraint, refines the merge, and projects the result to a DAG. We evaluate on Asia, Child, and an Alzheimer's disease graph with 100 samples and GPT-4o-mini. Over five seeds on Alzheimer's and Child, GoT-CD gives the highest mean F1 score and the lowest mean structural Hamming distance of the LLM methods, with 95% intervals of the difference excluding zero in seven of eight comparisons, and it returns a DAG in every run while using three LLM requests per graph. Replaying the logged runs without individual components attributes most of the gain to generating and merging several complete candidates. A case study on the effect of Sex on MOCA Score in the Alzheimer's graph shows the limits of structural scores: the fairness verdict drawn from the discovered graph disagrees with the reference verdict in twelve of fifteen LLM runs, including all five GoT-CD runs, which mostly drop the edge out of Sex. Graphs meant for a specific downstream analysis should therefore also be checked on the pathways that analysis depends on.

Machine Learning.title: When Does Learning to Stop Help? Configuring Risk-Controlled Early Exit for Reasoning-Model Services
Machine Learning.summary: Early exit lowers the cost of serving a reasoning model by stopping its reasoning once a provisional answer looks final. An operator must choose between a learned stopping rule and one static token budget, and savings against full reasoning do not settle the choice. We present a procedure that decides on calibration data from the workload. It certifies both families with Learn-then-Test to one bound on the fraction of all questions that full reasoning answers correctly but early exit does not, prices provisional answers as the serving stack does, and deploys the cheapest certified candidate. Across four models and five benchmarks neither family is better throughout. At a 5% risk target the learned rule saves 10.4-17.0 percentage points more tokens than the static budget on free-form mathematics with Qwen3, with accuracy 2.4-2.9 points below full reasoning, and less on MMLU-Pro on average. Which family costs less also changes with the risk target, in 8 of 15 settings, and with the price of a provisional answer. Across three prices, committing to one family in advance gives up as much as 27.4 points on some workload, whereas selecting on calibration data falls at most 11.6 points short of the better family, on a task with only 99 calibration questions. In a vLLM engine with Qwen3-8B, mean response time fell in proportion to generated tokens. Policies served on a task other than their calibration task exceeded the risk target in 18 of 44 task pairs; recalibration on the new task restored risk control.

Machine Learning.title: Predicting Lost Updates Is Not Enough to Choose a Rounding Policy
Machine Learning.summary: In low-precision training, a weight can round back to its previous value after a small update. We test whether predicting how often this happens helps choose a rounding rule. In Pythia-410M continuations from a common checkpoint, a higher-precision pilot accurately predicted the fraction of matrix weights left unchanged at each of the first 64 updates. Across three schedules with optimizer state retained or reset, nearest rounding gave lower validation loss at 256 updates than stochastic rounding or retaining 32-bit weights. The same ordering held at 512 updates with retained state. Accurately forecasting the unchanged fraction did not identify a benefit from switching policies in these runs.
Machine Learning.comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. This version adds matched Pythia-410M continuations under three weight-update policies, a paired optimizer-state comparison, and a 512-update extension. Ancillary files provide numerical data and replay scripts for all 36 runs

Machine Learning.title: Synthetic Crystal Data Generation for Diffusion Pretraining in Material Property Prediction
Machine Learning.summary: Diffusion-based pretraining has emerged as a powerful strategy for learning transferable representations in graph neural networks for materials property prediction without requiring quantum-mechanical labels such as energies, forces, and stresses for every pretraining structure. However, the method retains a critical dependency: it requires structures residing near local minima of a potential energy surface, which have traditionally been obtained through costly DFT relaxations of known or physically synthesized compounds. This reliance constrains both the scale and the structural diversity of available pretraining data, leaving large regions of crystal structure space unexplored. In this work, we connect diffusion-based pretraining with synthetic structure generation to reduce this bottleneck. We introduce a synthetic data generation pipeline combining three complementary strategies: perturb-and-relax, generative sampling via MatterGen, and protostructure enumeration. Where structural relaxation is required, we use fast machine-learned interatomic potentials instead of performing a new DFT relaxation for each generated structure. We further compare a coordinate-denoising control with continuous-time variance-preserving (VP) and sub-VP diffusion objectives using a randomly initialized Orb-v2 backbone. The source comparison covers seven MatBench property-prediction tasks, and an eighth task, \texttt{mp\_gap}, is included in the protostructure scaling study. Every synthetic-pretraining condition numerically outperforms random initialization on all seven source-comparison tasks. Scaling the protostructure corpus from 20k to 165k under a fixed 400-epoch schedule numerically matches or exceeds MP-20k pretraining on most tasks; because this protocol increases both data diversity and optimization updates, the result reflects joint data-and-compute scaling.
Machine Learning.comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: CoSlice: Coordinated Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for 5G Network Slicing Allocation
Machine Learning.summary: Radio Access Network (RAN) slicing is a shared resource allocation problem: each slice seeks to satisfy its Service Level Agreement (SLA) with minimal radio-resource consumption, while all slices compete for a limited resource budget. This creates both an intra-slice trade-off between SLA assurance and resource efficiency and an inter-slice conflict over shared resources, calling for specialized yet coordinated control. In this work, we present CoSlice, a coordinated multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for inter-slice physical resource block allocation in Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN). CoSlice uses preference-conditioned slice agents for fast resource allocation and an LLM-based coordinator to adapt their objectives using global network observations at a slower timescale. We formulate the problem as a multi-objective partially observable stochastic game (mo-POSG), establish the existence of a Preference Correlated Equilibrium, and derive a sublinear regret bound for the learning procedure. We implement the algorithm by using a two-stage training procedure that consists of multi-objective pretraining and joint optimization. We build a network slicing evaluation environment using ORANSlice and its radio-frequency simulator (RFsim), supporting realistic protocol-stack execution and application traffic across multiple slices. Experimental results show that CoSlice reduces both average and tail SLA violations compared with other centralized and multi-agent baselines under diverse slice workloads.

Machine Learning.title: Kernel Ridge Attention: Nonlinear Memory with Selective Forgetting
Machine Learning.summary: Kernel Ridge Attention (KRA) is a recurrent sequence mixer that combines learned nonlinear features with covariance-guided memory updates. It stores associations through recursive ridge regression, using correlations among past keys to determine how new observations modify memory. A content-dependent Ornstein--Uhlenbeck transition controls retention and restores uncertainty for future writes. This construction admits an exact temporal-kernel interpretation and maintains an inference state whose size is independent of context length. Associative block maps and explicit adjoints support parallel training while preserving the recursive update. In controlled language-modeling experiments, KRA improves prediction quality over attention and recurrent baselines, strengthens natural associative recall over the evaluated recurrent models, and achieves practical distributed training throughput. These properties provide a principled foundation for nonlinear, adaptive sequence memory.

Machine Learning.title: StreamPhy: Streaming Inference of High-Dimensional Physical Dynamics via State Space Models
Machine Learning.summary: Inferring the evolution of high-dimensional and multi-modal (e.g., spatio-temporal) physical fields from irregular sparse measurements in real time is a fundamental challenge in science and engineering. Existing approaches, including diffusion-based generative models and functional tensor methods, typically operate in offline settings, depend on full temporal observations, or incur substantial inference cost. We propose StreamPhy, an end-to-end framework that enables efficient and accurate streaming inference of full-field physical dynamics from incoming irregular sparse measurements. The framework integrates a data-adaptive observation encoder that is robust to arbitrary observation patterns, a structured state-space model that supports memory-efficient online updates across irregular time intervals, and an expressive Functional Tensor Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FT-FiLM) decoder for continuous-field generation. We prove that FT-FiLM is more expressive than the functional Tucker model, admitting a richer function class for handling complex dynamics. Experiments on three representative physical systems under challenging sampling patterns show that StreamPhy consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with at least 48\% improvement in accuracy and up to 20--100X faster inference than diffusion-based methods.

Machine Learning.title: Auditing Path-Specific Fairness Across Causal Discovery Algorithms: A Heart Failure Case Study
Machine Learning.summary: Causal discovery is increasingly applied to healthcare data, where the recovered relationships can encode biased pathways that propagate to downstream prediction. Path-specific fairness analysis, through direct, indirect, and spurious effect decompositions along with fairness-utility ratio assessment allows bias quantification and associated prediction cost. However, existing evaluations of causal discovery under fairness constraints have largely used non-clinical datasets and have not separated the contribution of confounders from that of mediators, leaving open how discovery-algorithm choice propagates through path-specific fairness to the utility trade-off in clinical settings. This work addresses that gap by establishing an expert-elicited causal graph benchmark for the heart failure clinical records dataset and tracing discovery algorithms through composite, per-variable fairness decompositions and fairness-utility ratio. ICA-LiNGAM achieves the lowest structural Hamming distance and highest recall, while GES achieves the highest precision. For path-specific effects, there was a 1.2 percentage-point difference in the mediated effect on ejection fraction on overall causal fairness between the original and discovered graphs. This ultimately led to variations in the fairness-utility ratio highlighting need for fine-grained evaluation. These results indicate that discovery-aware, path-specific fairness evaluation is consequential in clinical settings and warrants inclusion in routine auditing of clinical risk models.

Machine Learning.title: Accelerating Distributed Digital Ising Machines
Machine Learning.summary: Ising machines, dedicated accelerators built around the dynamics of Ising-like spin models, have emerged as a leading platform for combinatorial optimization and probabilistic sampling. The problems that motivate them require millions of spins, far beyond the on-chip capacity of any single device, so a practical Ising machine must distribute its computation across many devices. Prior work reports throughput at a single operating point, leaving the binding resource unidentified and platform crossovers measurable only by experiment; no calibrated cross-platform cost model of distributed Ising machines has been reported, nor have systematic techniques to accelerate their Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) workloads. This work presents a calibrated cost model that decomposes digital Ising sweep time into compute, memory, synchronization, and inter-device communication terms, validated with 4.8% mean error across three GPU generations, FPGA and ASIC up to 1 million spins. Guided by the model, we address each term in turn and propose: (i) a data placement strategy, worth up to 4.2$\times$ speedup; (ii) multi-rate and bounded-staleness schedules that relax the barrier that Gibbs sampling imposes, cutting time-to-solution (TTS) by up to 3.16$\times$ on three benchmarks; and (iii) a phase-offset streaming dataflow that hides boundary exchange behind interior computation whenever a link satisfies a latency-transparency criterion, yielding up to 1.25$\times$/1.74$\times$/2.01$\times$ on an H200 pair, a ZCU106 pair, and a four-board XEM8320 $2{\times}2$ mesh. The streaming dataflow is also implemented on a fabricated four-chip 28 nm ASIC sustaining 28.1 Gflips/s at 4.81 pJ/flip.

Machine Learning.title: A Rank-One Bypass of Fixed Linear Erasure
Machine Learning.summary: Linear concept erasure can make a target unreadable to a specified family of linear classifiers applied to a model's current internal features. In an open-weight release, however, an attacker can modify the layers that produce those features. We study a fixed affine erasure layer whose upstream model is allowed to change. If the layer transmits even one direction visible to an allowed downstream classifier, the attacker can write a target score into that direction and carry it through the layer. We show that this condition is also necessary, and that for a nonconstant linear target score the required change is a rank-one affine update. Across six CIFAR-10 class-pair tasks, the route restores nearly all pre-erasure target performance and can leave a deployed benign linear head's scores unchanged to numerical tolerance. We then price the attack: with eight target labels and 2,000 unlabelled calibration examples, a 10% mean relative feature edit yields 79.8% test accuracy, which is 91.2% of the fitted score's gain over chance; tighter edit limits sharply reduce success. Linear guardedness therefore remains a valid guarantee about the current representation, but it is not by itself a tamper-resistance guarantee for an editable open-weight model.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Child Safety in AI (poster). 10 pages, 3 figures

Machine Learning.title: OracleZoom: Reference-Constrained Recursive Image Super-Resolution Beyond Ground Truth
Machine Learning.summary: Recursive image Super-Resolution (SR) reaches extreme magnification by feeding each prediction back into the same model, like zooming into an image again and again. Real ground truth for deep zooms is impractical to capture (a full $256\times$ target would be a 52 GB image), so predictions at deeper zooms have no supervision. Yet the last ground-truth image still contains the region that every deeper zoom magnifies. OracleZoom turns this region into a training signal. Inspired by on-policy self-distillation, the model trains on its own prediction for one recursive step ($4\times \rightarrow 16\times$), and a cross-scale loss projects each $16\times$ prediction back to the last ground truth at $4\times$. This projection can verify only coarse content, so a no-reference quality objective guides the remaining fine detail, and a latent prior stops this objective from adding hallucinated artifacts. On seven datasets, OracleZoom achieves the highest CLIPIQA at every zoom depth (mean 0.713 vs. 0.621 for Chain-of-Zoom), with the largest gains at the deepest zooms, even though training stops at $16\times$ and optimizes a different quality metric. Pooled over two ground-truth-anchored judges, this added detail comes at the same hallucination rate as Chain-of-Zoom at $16\times$ and a lower rate at $4\times$, and removing the cross-scale loss raises hallucination at $16\times$.

Machine Learning.title: Infinity-Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Principal Component Analysis: Exact Reformulation, Finite-Sample Guarantee, and Efficient Algorithm
Machine Learning.summary: Principal component analysis (PCA) is a fundamental and ubiquitous technique for dimension reduction and representation learning, yet its empirical formulation remains vulnerable to distributional uncertainty. While distributionally robust optimization (DRO) offers a natural remedy, existing order-2 Wasserstein models of PCA either preserve the nominal PCA subspace or lack an exact reformulation. This paper demonstrates how the infinity-Wasserstein distance can reconcile these two desirable properties. For the resulting DRO model of PCA, we derive an exact finite-dimensional reformulation and explicitly identify a worst-case distribution attaining the inner maximum. Crucially, the reformulated objective retains samplewise residual information beyond the empirical covariance matrix, revealing a mechanism through which distributional robustness can reshape the learned principal subspace. Under the mild assumption that the true distribution has a finite fourth moment, we further establish a uniform finite-sample performance guarantee for the proposed model. An iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization algorithm is also developed to solve the resulting nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization problem, with a rigorous analysis of its convergence properties. Numerical experiments substantiate the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm and the practical effectiveness of the infinity-Wasserstein model in downstream applications.

Machine Learning.title: MIST: Reliable Streaming Decision Trees for Online Class-Incremental Learning via McDiarmid Bound
Machine Learning.summary: Streaming decision trees are natural candidates for open-world continual learning, as they perform local updates, enjoy bounded memory, and static decision boundaries. Despite these, they still fail in online class-incremental learning due to two coupled miscalibrations: (i) their split criterion grows unreliable as the class count K expands, and (ii) the absence of knowledge transfer at split time. Both failures share a common root: the range of Information Gain intrinsically scales with log2 K. Consequently, any Hoeffding-style confidence radius derived from it must inevitably grow with the class count, making a K-independent split criterion structurally impossible, taking away the potential benefits of applying streaming decision trees to continual learning. To fix this issue, we present MIST (McDiarmid Incremental Streaming Tree), which resolves both failures through three integrated components: (i) a tight, K-independent McDiarmid confidence radius for Gini splitting that acts as a structural regulariser; (ii) a Bayesian inheritance protocol that projects parent statistics to child nodes via truncated-Gaussian moments, with variance reduction guarantees strongest precisely when splitting is most conservative; and (iii) per-leaf KLL quantile sketches that support both continuous threshold evaluation and geometry-adaptive leaf prediction from a single data structure. On standard and stress-test tabular streams, MIST is competitive with global parametric methods on near-Gaussian benchmarks and uniquely robust on non-Gaussian geometry where SOTA benchmarks collapse.

Machine Learning.title: In Situ Training of Optical Neural Networks by Coding Agents
Machine Learning.summary: Optical neural networks promise fast, energy-efficient computing, but every device departs from its design and must be trained with the hardware. In situ training relies on an expert-built calibrated digital model of each device or on gradient-free trial and error. Coding agents, large language models that write and run programs, have shown an emergent ability to understand and edit the weights of digital neural networks. Here we introduce optics as code, a method in which a coding agent trains an optical neural network from measurements alone, through a harness that returns camera images of its probes and requires a hypothesis per request. We discovered that the agent forms a physical understanding of the optics and reparametrizes the network with interpretable optical elements tuned on the hardware. It outperforms gradient-free methods in classification and image encoding, approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at a fraction of the cost. Needing neither per-device calibration nor gradients through the hardware, and improving with more capable models, optics as code offers a practical route to large, scalable optical neural networks and a general tool for calibrating and optimizing optical experiments.
Machine Learning.comment: 14 pages, 4 figures. Our project website is at https://ioguz.github.io/optics-as-code/

Machine Learning.title: QAdapt: Noise-Adaptive Neural Pre-Decoding for Surface-Code Quantum Error Correction
Machine Learning.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing relies on quantum error correction to protect logical information, requiring classical decoders that keep pace with syndrome generation. Heterogeneous, changing hardware noise and the distribution shift from simulation to experiment challenge the accuracy and robustness of fixed neural decoders. We present QAdapt, a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction. QAdapt learns local spatiotemporal correlations, continually adapts across noise environments, and passes the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder. Online elastic weight consolidation limits forgetting as training moves between measurement, idle, CNOT, and Pauli-bias noise regimes. At distance nine, the HTNet pre-decoder reduces equivalent per-round logical error by 15.64% relative to Ising-Fast, with 28.75% fewer parameters and 9.07% less matching-backend time. Online EWC reduces average forgetting by 76.52% relative to sequential fine-tuning. With weights frozen, it reduces equivalent per-round logical error by 5.66% relative to continued base-environment training on a fixed valid domain of 331 unseen compound-noise conditions; whole-sequence failure probability falls by 2.54% over all 396 conditions. On native Willow records, the corresponding per-round reductions are 19.44%, 17.47%, and 17.95% at 10, 30, and 50 rounds, without target-domain fine-tuning. These results show how adaptive neural pre-decoding can improve logical accuracy, preserve performance across noise regimes, and reduce residual matching workload within an established decoding pipeline.
Machine Learning.comment: 16 pages, 11 figures, 4 tables, including appendices. Revised and expanded version

Machine Learning.title: Bad Genius: Counterfactual-Guided Harness Evolution Beyond Task-Specific Shortcuts
Machine Learning.summary: An optimized agent harness can improve on held-out tasks by relying on formatting conventions that those tasks share with the rest of the benchmark. We introduce Counterfactual Harness Search and Evolution (CHASE) to test whether harness improvements survive changes to the evaluation protocol. A Proposer edits the harness around a fixed foundation model. A Challenger then searches for a protocol change that preserves the tasks but reduces the updated harness's gain over the initial harness. Executable checks test whether the transformation preserves task semantics. If the gain loss is confirmed on held-out tasks, CHASE adds the transformation to an archive that constrains subsequent harness updates. We give conditions under which this finite archive bounds the gain loss on an ideal benchmark with shortcuts removed. We evaluate CHASE on Syn-Ledger, OfficeQA, FinanceBench, and SWE-Bench Pro V2. On Syn-Ledger, removing the known shortcuts yields 38.30% accuracy for CHASE and 18.27% for HarnessEvolve. On the 21 certification tasks from SWE-Bench Pro V2 HARD-51, changing the issue formatting and tool-output field order reduces HarnessEvolve's gain over the initial harness from 8.57 to 3.81 percentage points. The final CHASE harness retains 10.48 points of its 11.43-point gain under the same change.
Machine Learning.comment: 42 pages, 6 figures, including references and supplementary material

Machine Learning.title: Signature-Kernel Based Evaluation Metrics for Robust Probabilistic and Tail-Event Forecasting
Machine Learning.summary: Standard sample-based metrics like Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) and Quantile Loss (QL) are frequently used in the evaluation of probabilistic time-series forecasting. However, these metrics fail to capture multivariate correlations or assess the ability to capture distribution tails. These global metrics are insensitive to errors on high-utility events in distributional tails due to over-representation of the distribution's body. To accurately measure distributional fidelity on tail-regions and regions of high utility while still having a proper scoring rule, we introduce a family of censored signature kernel metrics. Our proposed metrics concentrate evaluation of forecasts to a focus region, representing high-utility or distributional tails, by collapsing the body of the distribution to a single pivot. Our benchmarks on time-series foundation models (TSFMs) reveal that while a clear ranking can be formed for distribution capture, there is no clear winner for tasks like systemic load prediction. This indicates that models with a strong ability to capture an overall distribution do not produce forecasts with high downstream utility. To encourage the use of the proposed metrics we open-source the efficient signature kernel (ESK) library. This library facilitates batch computation, with custom triton kernels, achieving a speed-up of up to 3.58$\times$ compared to implementations via the popular SigKernel library. Code for our metrics are available on GitHub.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted as a poster at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track) Main Paper: 10 pages 2 figures Including Appendix and References: 19 pages 7 figures

Machine Learning.title: One Checkpoint, Many Runs: Recipe Cards for Fine-Tuned Models
Machine Learning.summary: Fine-tuned language models are shared with model cards that describe the training setup in detail, often down to the default random seed, but report the score of a single released checkpoint. Such setups are retrained routinely, by fine-tuning services for each customer, by organizations at each update, and by users on their own data, so the model that is deployed comes from a new run of the setup. Some runs fail, and a failed run can go unnoticed and reach the people the model serves. We call such a setup a model recipe and argue that its documentation should state how often a run of the recipe misses a required performance bar. In a survey of the model cards of 300 fine-tuned language models on Hugging Face, none reports this failure probability, and only three report results from more than one training run. Across 2,124 fine-tuning runs, we find that reading the mean, the median, or a bootstrap interval as an approval often approves recipes whose failure rate exceeds a stated failure tolerance, because these summaries do not measure how often a run fails. Model cards do not report how often the runs of a recipe fail, although whoever runs the training is best placed to count them, while those who rely on a retrained model bear the cost of a failed run. To report this failure probability directly, we propose recipe cards, an addendum to model cards that documents the model recipe behind a checkpoint. A recipe card states the bar and the tolerance and who chose them, reports how many runs are made and how many of them miss the bar, gives an upper bound on the failure probability, and warns when this bound exceeds the tolerance. Recipe cards record who set and who accepted this risk, and let deployers and regulators state acceptance criteria for retrained models.

Machine Learning.title: What Does a Temporal Benchmark Score Measure? Decomposing Channel Use in Video VLM Evaluation
Machine Learning.summary: A score on a temporal video question answering benchmark is meant to measure that a model has temporal understanding, but it conflates two questions. (1)~is the question even temporal, does it need several frames and their order? And (2)~when it does, does the model recover the order from the pixels, or read it off the positional encoding (RoPE)? Most of a temporal score answers neither, since a single frame and answer priors often carry it, and the field's validity checks, frame-shuffle sensitivity and multi-frame gain, speak only to (1). For (2) we score a reversal conflict, frames reversed while RoPE stays forward, two ways: label-free, as the accuracy lost against the forward labels, and against reversed labels wherever labels transform deterministically under time reversal. This separates a model that follows the reversed content from one merely disrupted. The two readings dissociate two similarly scoring models at both model scales. Qwen3-VL answers the reversed event it actually sees, reading the visual sequence. Molmo2 correctly reports a backwards video when positions agree, and flipping only the RoPE indices flips its prediction to the forward events, i.e. it reads positions. We call these regimes \emph{visual-sequence-dominant} and \emph{position-dominant}. Controls show reversed content is processable whenever the channels agree, and that both families share a bias toward describing events as running forward (arrow-of-time prior) that, being similar in strength, cannot by itself account for the dissociation. The distinction matters because the two channels fail on opposite inputs: two models with the same score are not interchangeable.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027, Datasets and Evaluation Track

Machine Learning.title: FlashREINFORCE: Critic-Free Single-Rollout Asynchronous RL for Agentic Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning suits long-horizon agents with irregular rollout times, but group-relative updates require repeated rollouts of each prompt. However, group-based sampling limits prompt coverage at a fixed rollout budget and introduces group synchronization barriers. One rollout per prompt avoids these constraints but requires learning from stale, variable-length trajectories without a sibling baseline. We present FlashREINFORCE, to our knowledge the first critic-free single-rollout framework that scales to long asynchronous training and large models. It combines One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization, which provide prompt coverage and batch centering while controlling policy drift and length-amplified negative updates. Each component is easy to implement, and the result is their combination: a batch-mean baseline is stable under sample-mean loss, and each common alternative degrades or collapses training. FlashREINFORCE remains stable through 6,000 updates on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at policy lag four, and through 1,450 on the 30B MoE Qwen3-30B-A3B at lag eight. Under identical loss, data, and lag it matches a strengthened group-relative baseline within 0.5 points, and with half the rollouts exceeds published synchronous baselines on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B (38.0 versus 36.3 five-benchmark mean). On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct it maintains tool use where GRPO stops calling tools and achieves 98.3%/96.5% seen/unseen ALFWorld success.

Machine Learning.title: LAGR: Language-Aware Grasp Re-Ranking for Task Oriented Grasping
Machine Learning.summary: Grasping is a fundamental capability for robotic manipulation, with the appropriate grasp depending on the downstream task. For example, a hammer should be held by its handle for hammering but by its head when it is handed over. Selecting such a grasp requires consideration of two criteria: physical feasibility on the object and suitability for the task. Developing such an approach requires dense grasp labels with both feasibility and task scores on real observations, but existing task-oriented grasping datasets are small, synthetic, or costly to annotate. To address this gap, we construct a dataset of 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations over 100,911 image-task pairs from $17$ object categories. Additionally, we introduce LAGR, a task-oriented grasp detection method that explicitly addresses both these challenges. Given vision-language inputs, LAGR first generates task-independent grasp proposals along with a physical feasibility score, and then scores the generated grasps with a language-conditioned re-ranker that reasons over all proposals jointly. Experiments show that LAGR outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points. We further validate LAGR on real objects by executing task-oriented grasps with a Franka Research 3 robot.
Machine Learning.comment: Manav Kulshrestha and Shreyans Jain contributed equally to this work

Machine Learning.title: MOLT: A Hugging Face-Native, Minimal, and Scalable Framework for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) research iterates quickly on agents, rewards, and learning algorithms, while policies have grown to hundreds of billions of parameters and beyond. Existing open frameworks force a choice: those that are easy to modify do not scale to the largest models, and those that scale rely on Megatron, which needs dedicated bridge code for every model family and several times more framework code. We present MOLT, an open-source framework built for research that is Hugging Face-native, minimal, and scalable. Its code is easy to modify: the entire RL path is approximately 9.2K lines of Python with one training backend and one rollout engine, so a researcher or an AI coding agent can read it in full and edit the code that actually runs. A Hugging Face checkpoint is loaded directly into a PyTorch FSDP2 trainer with tensor, expert, and context parallelism, so a new model family needs no bridge, and the same code scales from a 4B model to a 753B one. Existing OpenAI- and Anthropic-SDK agents are trained by redirecting their client, with automatic handling of agents that rewrite their own context; training is fully asynchronous; and trajectory data stay in a distributed object store. With MOLT, a 30B mixture-of-experts tool agent trains stably for 1,464 asynchronous updates, a visual computer-use agent improves on OSWorld, asynchronous training is 2.40 times faster than synchronous training, and pipeline throughput reaches 92% of a Megatron-based stack. Its trainer, NeMo AutoModel, trains models of one to 2.8 trillion parameters.
Machine Learning.comment: Technical report. Code: https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/labs-molt. Documentation: https://nvidia-nemo.github.io/labs-molt/guide/. Demonstration video: https://youtu.be/3DqXGFIce0o

Machine Learning.title: Neural Memory Orchestration
Machine Learning.summary: Modern HPC workloads increasingly stall on the memory hierarchy rather than on compute, and page faults from mmap'd files, swap, and tiered memory are a growing fraction of wall time. Heuristic prefetchers in the kernel handle stride-like and temporally clustered patterns well but degrade sharply on the irregular, data-dependent access streams typical of these workloads. Learned prefetchers have been shown to capture such patterns in simulation but have not been taken to a deployed pipeline running against live workloads on real hardware. We present Overseer, an end-to-end learned page-prefetching system. An eBPF collector observes page faults on the target host, a transformer predictor (OverNet) runs on network-attached inference hardware and emits future page addresses, and a kernel-resident enforcer materializes those pages into the target's address space before they are demanded. OverNet encodes fault sequences through per-instance ordinal ranks over deltas, which lets a single trained model serve any target process without retraining. On two page-fault-heavy workloads, Overseer reduces runtime by roughly 35% on Hilbert-curve traversal and by roughly an order of magnitude on dense matrix multiplication, with corresponding reductions in major-fault counts.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Cross-Modal Reconstruction: Participant-Level Evaluation of sEMG-Kinematic Coupling in Post-Stroke Gait
Machine Learning.summary: Accurate cross-modal reconstruction is often treated as evidence of physiological coupling, although it may simply reflect temporal patterns shared across participants. We tested whether frozen bidirectional models captured subject-specific neuromuscular coupling between electromyographic activity and gait kinematics in 82 held-out able-bodied and 43 post-stroke participants. Complete source-modality removal and cross-participant source substitution, along with a cycle-position-age-sex template baseline, were applied. Learned bilateral asymmetry was also compared with transparent waveform and derivative asymmetry for predicting Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA) scores in the case of repeated nested cross-validation. Complete source removal increased reconstruction RMSE by 6.90% for electromyography-to-kinematics and 11.38% in the reverse direction. In contrast, cross-participant substitution increased RMSE by only 1.68% and 1.67%, respectively, while the template reduced RMSE by 2.89% and 0.55%. For POMA prediction, walking speed, age, and sex achieved an MAE of 3.693, compared with 4.229 and 4.427 after adding absolute and signed learned asymmetry, respectively. In all of the 20 repeated evaluations, all asymmetry representations performed worse than the covariate baseline. No localized learned feature remained significant after covariate adjustment and false-discovery-rate correction. The model mainly relied on shared gait-phase patterns, with no clear subject-specific coupling or added clinical value. Participant-level controls are therefore needed before reconstruction accuracy is treated as evidence of individualized physiology.

Machine Learning.title: Don't Pay Attention, PLANT It: Pretraining Attention via Learning-to-Rank
Machine Learning.summary: State-of-the-art Extreme Multi-Label Text Classification models rely on multi-label attention to focus on key tokens in input text, but learning good attention weights is challenging. We introduce PLANT (Pretrained and Leveraged AtteNTion), a plug-and-play strategy for initializing the label-attention module that operates on top of an LLM's output representations. PLANT works by planting label-specific attention using a Learning-to-Rank model trained on mutual information gain, before end-to-end fine-tuning. This architecture-agnostic approach integrates with LLM backbones (e.g., Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-V3, and Phi-3-mini). PLANT outperforms SOTA methods across tasks like ICD coding, legal topic classification, and content recommendation, and improves fine-tuned LLMs in controlled comparisons outside the medical domain. Gains are largest on rare labels, although a training-free LLM extraction baseline remains competitive on rarely seen labels. Ablation studies confirm that attention initialization is a key driver of these gains. We make our code available at https://github.com/deb-official/plant
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. v5 is the camera-ready version, revised after the NeurIPS reviews: new comparisons with fine-tuned LLMs outside the medical domain and with zero- and few-shot LLM baselines. 41 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. Code: https://github.com/deb-official/plant

Machine Learning.title: A Fast, Programmable GPU-to-CPU Invocation Layer for GPU-Initiated Communication
Machine Learning.summary:
Modern GPU workloads increasingly rely on device-initiated communication to let GPU kernels communicate directly without synchronizing with the host at kernel boundaries. Existing libraries commonly favor placing transport control on GPU threads, an approach known as GPUDirect Async (GDA), and treat reverse offload to host proxy threads as a slower fallback. We argue that reverse offload can outperform GDA and should be a first-class communication path. We further propose exposing reverse offload as a programming interface that lets users define workload-specific communication operations.
  We present KIWI, a programmable reverse-offload framework that achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second. We address practical challenges of scaling reverse offload, including contention on shared queues, polling overhead, and load imbalance across proxies. KIWI-P2P, a SHMEM-like library built on KIWI, outperforms state-of-the-art GDA implementations in both latency and bandwidth. More importantly, KIWI-EP redesigns low-latency mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine kernels around workload-defined operations, lowering expert-parallel communication latency by up to 2.3x over the best existing backend on AMD GPUs and time per output token in vLLM by up to 29%. The source code of KIWI is available at https://github.com/AMDResearch/kiwi.

Machine Learning.title: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
Machine Learning.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.
Machine Learning.comment: Apoorva Vashisth and Manav Kulshrestha contributed equally to this work. Prof. Zachary Kingston and Prof. Aniket Bera jointly advised this work

Machine Learning.title: Online State-Representation Adaptation under Synthetic Interaction-Cue Remapping
Machine Learning.summary: When cues change what they predict, continuing to update a learned mapping may help an agent choose the appropriate action. We tested this in a one-step synthetic task by comparing a logistic state predictor that continued to learn from state labels with the same predictor frozen at transfer. We evaluated ten conditions in six held-out environments, with 1,296 paired runs per condition and 1,296,000 transfer records in total. Late action accuracy was 93.39% with online updates and 64.63% with frozen coefficients, a paired difference of 28.76 [8.73, 53.19] percentage points (95% environment-bootstrap interval). A direct policy reached 95.65% using the same predictions with a different action threshold. A contextual bandit reached 94.23% and earned more cumulative utility than the adaptive predictor. The bandit used the reward of its chosen action, which in this task reveals the true state when combined with that action. Weights based on development history lowered cumulative utility relative to neutral weights (difference -3.45 [-4.48, -2.43]). The adaptive predictor outperformed its frozen counterpart in late accuracy in each of the six test environments. The other comparisons show how the choice of action threshold and the information available in feedback affect what can be attributed to online adaptation.
Machine Learning.comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Code and synthetic data are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24329690

Machine Learning.title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
Machine Learning.summary: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.

Machine Learning.title: Think Before You Distill: Generalization Recovery in Quantized VLAs via Selective Policy Distillation
Machine Learning.summary: Post-training quantization has been shown to preserve VLA performance under standard evaluation conditions, but whether it preserves the full-precision model's robustness and generalization remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically study the robustness and generalization of post-quantized VLA policies under environmental disturbances. Empirical results show that quantized policies can become fragile to subtle environmental variations despite retaining comparable in-distribution performance. We further observe that action discrepancies are concentrated in a small subset of the rollout states, while teacher guidance has opposite effects depending on discrepancy: it improves performance at high-discrepancy states but can degrade it at low-discrepancy states. These findings reveal that effective post-quantization recovery requires selective intervention on vulnerable states rather than globally distilling the student. We therefore propose Policy-Induced Vulnerability-Oriented Tuning (PIVOT-Q), a vulnerability-aware On-Policy Distillation (OPD) framework that selectively corrects vulnerable states encountered during quantized-student rollouts using the frozen full-precision policy as a teacher. PIVOT-Q identifies vulnerable states using discounted accumulated discrepancies over a short horizon, applies phase-balanced sparse supervision, and uses a Behavioral Anchor to prevent unintended changes. Experiments under seven LIBERO-Plus environmental variations demonstrate consistent recovery across multiple VLA backbones and quantization methods. Notably, PIVOT-Q outperforms full-state distillation with smaller variance across evaluated settings while using only 20\% of its state-level distillation budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/ruanruan-andy/PIVOT-Q.

Machine Learning.title: CAFE-AQI: Coverage-Aware Day-Ahead AQI Forecasting with Early Warning and Conformal Uncertainty in Bangladesh
Machine Learning.summary: Next-day air quality forecasting often assumes city records are equally complete and independent. However, an audit of a large Bangladesh dataset revealed a sharp coverage expansion after August 2022 and showed that 103 city labels correspond to only 61 unique AQI trajectories. To address these issues, this paper presents CAFE-AQI, a coverage-aware framework for forecasting next-day maximum AQI. It also estimates the probability of Unhealthy-or-worse conditions (AQI >= 151). Data were divided chronologically into training (2022-2023), calibration (2024), and testing (2025). To prevent duplicate records from dominating training and evaluation, identical trajectories were weighted. The framework combines temporal and pollutant features with a five-neighbor spatial context. It also includes a class-balanced warning head and risk-conditional conformal calibration aimed at providing early warnings and prediction intervals. Evaluation on the duplicate-balanced 2025 data gave an MAE of 9.76, an RMSE of 15.04, and an R-squared value of 0.910 for CAFE-AQI. Its MAE was 3.63 AQI lower than persistence (95% CI: 3.49-3.76), with lower errors in each of the 61 trajectory groups. For unhealthy-air warnings, the F1-score was 0.908 and the AUROC was 0.982. The nominal 90% intervals covered 92.09% of observations. When an entire spatial block was excluded from training, the MAE remained 10.66, showing that the lightweight model transferred reasonably well to unseen locations.

Machine Learning.title: The Effectiveness and Durability of Pretraining Data Filtering in Protein Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Pretraining filtering is one of the most common safeguards for open-weight language models. Here we study its effectiveness, durability and scalability using the ESM-2 family of protein language models. We find that filtering viral proteins from the pretraining data meaningfully degrades masked language modelling, mutation effect prediction and long-range contact prediction on viral proteins, while largely preserving performance on non-viral proteins. These effects are concentrated among proteins from human-infecting viruses, and grow as we scale models from 8M to 3B parameters. As models increase in size, we find that stringent filtering becomes more effective. However, fine-tuning on sequences from the removed viral families restores the lost performance. Although the cost to recover performance increases with model scale, even for the largest models it costs about 80 USD of H100 time. This work establishes pretraining filtering as moderately effective at selectively degrading performance on viral proteins, but not durable against fine-tuning with modest computational resources and access to relevant data.

Machine Learning.title: Continual Tool-Space Extension Learning for Multimodal Agents
Machine Learning.summary: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

Machine Learning.title: Sightline: Long-Window Speculative Decoding for Fast SVG Generation
Machine Learning.summary: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation models write a graphic as code with one forward pass per token, so drawing is slow. Speculative decoding speeds them up losslessly, and block drafters guess many tokens per pass. On SVG, many of their rounds accept the whole draft and end only at the verification window. We find that their misses are rare and clumped, and that they stay accurate far deeper into a block than on natural language. A run-length identity and three propositions show that a longer window pays once the candidates are wide, up to the drafter's horizon. We propose Sightline, which pairs a window as long as the drafter's horizon with a draft tree wide enough to fill it. Experiments cover text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG with three models on six benchmarks from MMSVG, MMSVG-2M and SArena. In every setting, Sightline is the fastest of the compared lossless decoders. On SArena, it stays the fastest when every decoder shares one loop control. It also leads in almost every setting of six models from four other families, which write SVG code, compressed SVG tokens or Lottie JSON. Analyses trace the lead to rounds that shorter windows cut off, both in loop-free content and in loops. Speculative decoding also saves time for choosing samples by rendering, which beats choosing by likelihood. These results suggest that speculative decoding on vector graphics should verify as far as the drafter sees. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/Sightline.

Machine Learning.title: Improved Leverage Score Sampling for Constrained Active Linear Regression
Machine Learning.summary: In this paper we study active learning for constrained linear regression. Given a design matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, a constraint set $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, and query access to $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we seek an approximate solution to $\min_{x\in C}\|Ax-b\|_2^2$ using as few queries as possible. This problem arises in many scientific and engineering applications, and randomized leverage score sampling provides a powerful method to solve it. However, existing leverage score methods ignore the constraint or encode it through ridge regularization, suffering unfavorable query complexity for anisotropic constraint sets. We propose ellipsoid-regularized leverage scores, where we approximate the constraint set by an outer ellipsoid and use its shape matrix to bias sampling toward directions that matter under the constraint geometry. We prove that the query complexity is governed by an anisotropic effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}(C)\le d$. With appropriate parameters, $O(d_{\text{eff}}(C)\log d/\varepsilon^2)$ queries suffice to return a point in $C$ with objective value at most $(1+\varepsilon)$ times the optimum. This bound can substantially improve on the standard leverage-score bound, since anisotropic constraints can make $d_{\text{eff}}(C)$ much smaller than $d$. For convex constraints, we improve the dependence on $\varepsilon$ from $1/\varepsilon^2$ to $1/\varepsilon$. We also prove two lower bounds: first, the $d/\varepsilon^2$ dependence is unavoidable without convexity assumptions on $C$, and second, in some regimes, the effective dimension dependence $d_{\mathrm{eff}}(C)/\varepsilon$ is necessary for ellipsoidal constraints. Experiments on synthetic regression problems and a parametric heat conduction problem show lower regression error than standard baselines for similar query budget.

Machine Learning.title: Learning through Internalization
Machine Learning.summary: We study internalization processes, by which neural-network-based systems absorb an explicit computational procedure into their own weights, and how they facilitate learning. We investigate how transformers internalize the simulation of semiautomata by internalizing chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, which classes of semiautomata are harder to internalize, and expose the flip side of internalization, that is, a progressive degradation of out-of-distribution performance. We then provide the first provable analysis of successful internalization: for the task of learning parities, we show that a simplified one-layer transformer provably first learns the target with explicit CoT supervision and then internalizes the autoregressive generation as CoT tokens are progressively removed, learning to directly compute the parity. This task is computationally hard to learn from data without CoT supervision. Finally, we discuss how learning through internalization relates to the \textit{Positive Distribution Shift} phenomenon recently introduced by~\citet{Med+26}.

Machine Learning.title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.
Machine Learning.comment: 87 pages, 43 figures, including appendices and the NeurIPS paper checklist

Machine Learning.title: STORM: A Lightweight Structure-Free Model for Binding Affinity Prediction
Machine Learning.summary: Accurately predicting a small molecule's binding affinity to a protein, a critical task in drug discovery, remains challenging. Physics-based approaches like free-energy perturbation (FEP) have very high computational costs and require expert setup. Recent machine learning--based cofolding models have reported accuracy approaching that of FEP---and at least one of them, Boltz-2, has already been widely adopted for affinity prediction---but they remain expensive for large computational screens and even more expensive for retraining on newly collected experimental data. To address these challenges, we introduce STORM: Similarity Transfer from Observed Reference Molecules. STORM is a fast, simple machine learning model that ensembles many small model fusions of diverse protein and molecule representations for binding affinity prediction. Trained on the same data, STORM matches or exceeds the accuracy of Boltz-2 on multiple evaluation datasets, while delivering a speed improvement of over five orders of magnitude for both inference and training. Our results also suggest opportunities to substantially improve affinity prediction accuracy by integrating historical experimental affinity data with structural and biophysical information.

Machine Learning.title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$
Machine Learning.summary: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.
Machine Learning.comment: 57 pages, 17 figures, 7 tables. In the title, n-DAS denotes an optimizer of order n restricted to the dominant aligned subspace (DAS): 1-DAS for first-order and 2-DAS for second-order methods

Machine Learning.title: Imitation Learning from Human Motion Alone Does Not Guarantee Biomechanically Plausible Gait Kinetics
Machine Learning.summary: Imitation learning (IL) via motion data is increasingly used in robotics and character animation, yet its ability to be applied to human biomechanics to estimate physiologically plausible joint moments without explicit kinetic information remains unclear. In this study, we examined whether motion imitation alone can estimate reasonable biological joint moments in human walking. We compared motion-only IL (MOIL) against a kinetics-aware IL (KAIL) framework, which incorporates additional ground reaction forces (GRFs) and center of pressure (CoP) in imitation rewards. A progressive kinetic reward shaping approach was used to examine the contribution of each kinetic term. Experiments were conducted using walking data from two non-disabled participants at three speeds (0.9, 1.2, and 1.5 m/s). While both MOIL and KAIL achieved comparable kinematic tracking accuracy, KAIL produced kinetics more closely aligned with biomechanical values across participants and walking speeds, reducing the root mean square errors (RMSEs) of vertical GRF and CoP by 40% and 48%, and of hip, knee, and ankle moments by 19%, 18%, and 35%, respectively, relative to MOIL. These findings highlight a fundamental limitation of MOIL approaches, as their failure to accurately estimate human-like gait kinetics may lead to erroneous interpretations of gait biomechanics and adversely affect downstream applications such as wearable robot design and the diagnosis of pathological gait.

Machine Learning.title: Controllable Generative Trajectory Prediction via Weak Preference Alignment
Machine Learning.summary: Deep generative models such as conditional variational autoencoders (CVAEs) have shown great promise for predicting trajectories of surrounding agents in autonomous vehicle planning. State-of-the-art models have achieved remarkable accuracy in such prediction tasks. Besides accuracy, diversity is also crucial for safe planning because human behaviors are inherently uncertain and multimodal. However, existing methods generally lack a scheme to generate controllably diverse trajectories, which is arguably more useful than randomly diversified trajectories, to the end of safe planning. To address this, we propose PrefCVAE, an augmented CVAE framework that uses weakly labeled preference pairs to imbue latent variables with semantic attributes. Using average velocity as an example attribute, we demonstrate that PrefCVAE enables controllable, semantically meaningful predictions without degrading baseline accuracy. Our results show the effectiveness of preference supervision as a cost-effective way to enhance sampling-based generative models.

Machine Learning.title: Towards Generalizable Reasoning: Group Causal Counterfactual Policy Optimization for LLM Reasoning
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at complex tasks with advances in reasoning capabilities. However, existing reward mechanisms remain tightly coupled to final correctness and pay little attention to the underlying reasoning process: trajectories with sound reasoning but wrong answers receive low credit, while lucky guesses with flawed logic may be highly rewarded, affecting reasoning generalization. From a causal perspective, we interpret multi-candidate reasoning for a fixed question as a family of counterfactual experiments. Building on this, we propose Group Causal Counterfactual Policy Optimization to explicitly train LLMs to learn generalizable reasoning patterns. It proposes an episodic causal counterfactual reward that jointly captures (i) robustness, encouraging the answer distribution induced by a reasoning step to remain stable under counterfactual perturbations; and (ii) effectiveness, enforcing sufficient variability so that the learned reasoning strategy can transfer across questions. We then construct token-level advantages from this reward and optimize the policy, encouraging LLMs to favor reasoning patterns that are process-valid and counterfactually robust. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate its advantages.

Machine Learning.title: When Normal-Only Updates Are Not Enough: Test-Time Adaptation in Reconstruction-Based Time-Series Anomaly Detection
Machine Learning.summary: Normal operating conditions can evolve after deployment, motivating test-time adaptation (TTA) of time-series anomaly detectors using incoming data. Yet the same stream may contain anomalies, so TTA with online updates must decide which test samples should be used for adaptation. This leaves a more basic question: even if updates are restricted to samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, does TTA reliably improve anomaly detection? We study this question with a controlled intervention that replaces the practical update selector with a rule that uses only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, while keeping the rest of the online adaptation procedure unchanged. Across nine benchmark families, four optimizer configurations, and five random seeds, we obtain three main findings: (1) using only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark does not reliably improve detection; (2) practical TTA failures exhibit two distinct responses to this intervention, with 63 of 180 settings recovering a clear detection gain while 90 still show no clear detection gain; and (3) the updates reduce their immediate reconstruction objective across the evaluated settings, yet these reductions do not consistently lead to better anomaly ranking. Both failure patterns persist across alternative practical adaptation variants and modest perturbations of the benchmark labels. Together, these findings show that improving sample selection alone is not a complete solution to reconstruction-based TSAD TTA.

Machine Learning.title: Interpreting Timestamp Permutations in Dynamic Link Prediction
